![Longitudinal profile of a river: height above sea level against distance downstream from the source, 0 to 50 km](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.3-007-INTERP-question.png)

Describe the downstream gradient pattern in this longitudinal profile, using its height and distance scales.
items.canonical_answer:
The profile falls towards the downstream end, from 900 m at the source to 100 m at 50 km. It is steeper upstream and gentler downstream overall: it drops 400 m in the first 10 km (1:25) but only 100 m in the last 20 km (1:200). items.prompt:
![A river reach in three views: (a) a section along the river with a 4 m drop over resistant rock, (b) a plan view, (c) a cross-section X–Y](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.3-018-INTERP-question.png)

Describe the erosion landforms and process sequence shown in this figure, using its waterfall, plunge pool and gorge evidence.
items.canonical_answer:
The abrupt 4 m drop at the lip in section (a) identifies the waterfall, with a hollow at its foot as the plunge pool. The less resistant rock is cut back beneath the resistant cap, leaving an overhang, and blocks of the cap lie in the pool, so the unsupported cap collapses. Repeated undercutting and collapse let the waterfall retreat upstream, and the narrow, steep-sided reach left downstream (plan b, section c) is the gorge.

![Annotated waterfall, plunge pool and gorge](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.3-018-INTERP-answer.png)
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the waterfall/pool feature relationship; 1 for interpreting the undercut-collapse evidence; 1 for the retreat/gorge pattern in the figure.

items.prompt: Explain how a fall in the volume of water can make an ephemeral river deposit its load as it flows across a sandy, permeable bed.
items.canonical_answer: Water seeps into the sandy, permeable bed and evaporates, so the volume of flowing water falls downstream. With less water the river has less energy. It can no longer transport all its load, so it deposits the coarsest material first and, as the flow dies away, drops finer material on the bed as well.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for water loss by seepage into the permeable bed or evaporation as the causal factor; 1 for the link that less volume gives the river less energy; 1 for the effect that it cannot carry all its load and deposits it; 1 for explaining why coarse material is dropped first and finer material later as the flow dies away.

items.prompt: Explain how a road crossing with blocked openings can affect shallow wetland flow and how a targeted response could help.
items.canonical_answer: Blocked openings obstruct water movement, which can cause upstream ponding or redirected flow. Assessing and clearing suitable openings can restore connectivity, provided their capacity and position suit the flow. Performance needs checking during relevant conditions.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for obstruction as a cause; 1 for the flow-to-ponding/redirected-water link; 1 for clearing/assessing openings as a targeted response; 1 for the conditional connectivity effect and need to check performance.

items.prompt:
(a) Name the boundary separating neighbouring river basins. [1]
(b) Describe hydraulic action, abrasion and attrition by identifying the main contact in each. [3]
(c) Name the transport mode in which particles hop near the bed. [1]
(d) Describe two movement contrasts in this resource: A rolls while touching the bed; B remains as fine solid particles within the flowing water. [2]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Drainage divide/watershed. (b) Hydraulic action is water force on channel material; abrasion is load contacting and wearing the channel; attrition is particles colliding and wearing one another. (c) Saltation. (d) A is along-bed traction with contact; B is suspension within the water without continuing bed contact during the observation.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for the boundary name as the required point.
(b) 3 A marks for the three distinct action/contact descriptions; maximum one per process.
(c) 1 A mark for saltation.
(d) 2 B marks for interpreting the given movement points: along-bed rolling/contact at A and within-water suspended particles at B.

items.prompt:
An original river resource records: outer bend depth 2.4 m and speed 0.9 m/s; inner bend depth 0.8 m and speed 0.3 m/s with an exposed sand bar. A nearby flood deposit is 12 cm thick and coarse beside the channel, but 3 cm and finer farther away.
(a) Name the bend landform. [1]
(b) Describe the bend’s paired depth/speed pattern and process interpretation. [3]
(c) Describe how the flood-deposit pattern supports natural-levee development. [2]
(d) What judgement is supported about these observations proving a pattern in every season? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Meander. (b) The outer bank is deeper and faster using 2.4 m/0.9 m/s against 0.8 m/0.3 m/s; the inner side has a sand bar, supporting outer erosion opposite inner deposition. (c) Greater coarse near-channel accumulation contrasts with a thinner finer deposit farther away; repeated such events can build a river-side levee. (d) No: one set of observations does not establish all-season conditions.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for meander.
(b) 3 B marks for the depth comparison, speed comparison and process interpretation using the sand-bar evidence; retain units.
(c) 2 B marks for the coarse/thick versus fine/thin data contrast and its qualified connection to repeated levee building.
(d) 1 C mark for a supported decision that the observation window cannot prove every-season conditions.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that the oshanas of the Cuvelai system bring more benefits than problems to the people who live among them? [5]
items.canonical_answer: Partly agree. In the wet season the shallow oshanas fill with water that people use for livestock and household needs; they provide fish and support grazing and cultivation on the moist, low-lying ground, so many households depend on them. However, when large amounts of water flow in from Angola after heavy rain, oshanas can flood homes, schools, crops and roads, especially where people have built in channels that looked dry in earlier years. Standing water can also help spread disease where sanitation is poor, and roads without enough openings can make the flooding worse. The oshanas are a valuable resource, but whether the benefits outweigh the problems depends on the year and on where people build. With homes kept out of the flow paths and roads built with suitable culverts, the benefits can be greater than the problems.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging relevant evidence on both sides: benefits (seasonal water for livestock and households, fish, grazing, cultivation) and problems (flooding of homes, crops, schools and roads when inflow from Angola is high, building in dry channels, disease, obstruction by roads). Maximum 3 marks if only one side is judged.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision such as "partly agree", which may be implied; a bare agree or disagree earns no mark.
